text: A team added a Claude Code review step to its CI pipeline. The job starts but hangs until it times out, and no review is produced. What is the most likely fix?
options: Give the CI job a longer timeout so the review has time to finish
Move the review into a separate Claude Code session that runs on a server
Switch the review step to a larger, faster model so it finishes the work sooner
Run Claude Code with `-p` so it prints one result and exits without waiting
correct_answer: Run Claude Code with `-p` so it prints one result and exits without waiting
explanation: Without `-p` (`--print`), Claude Code starts an interactive session and waits for input that never comes in CI. Running it non-interactively with `-p` (D) returns one result and exits. A longer timeout (A) just waits longer. A separate server session (B) is over-engineering. A larger model (C) does not change the fact that the session is waiting for input.

text: A repository's API handlers have strict conventions that do not apply anywhere else. The team wants Claude Code to load those conventions only when it works on files under `src/api/`. Where should they go?
options: In a file under `.claude/rules/` with a `paths` glob for `src/api/**`
In the root `CLAUDE.md`, under a heading named API Handler Conventions
In each developer's personal `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` on their own machine
In a comment block at the top of every file inside the `src/api/` folder
correct_answer: In a file under `.claude/rules/` with a `paths` glob for `src/api/**`
explanation: A rule file in `.claude/rules/` with `paths` frontmatter (A) loads automatically only when Claude works on matching files, so unrelated sessions are not bloated. The root `CLAUDE.md` (B) loads in every session. Personal files (C) are not shared with the team. Comments in each file (D) are duplicated everywhere and easy to miss.

text: A team wants every developer who clones a repository to get the same build commands, coding conventions, and allowed test commands in Claude Code. Where should this configuration live?
options: In each developer's `~/.claude/settings.json` and `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` files
In the repository's committed `CLAUDE.md` and `.claude/settings.json` files
In `.claude/settings.local.json`, which each developer keeps in their own clone
In a team wiki page that developers paste into the start of each session
correct_answer: In the repository's committed `CLAUDE.md` and `.claude/settings.json` files
explanation: Team rules for one project belong in committed project files (B), so everyone who clones the repository gets them automatically. User files under `~/.claude/` (A) apply to one developer only. `settings.local.json` (C) is not committed and is meant for personal experiments. A wiki page (D) depends on every developer remembering to paste it.

text: Leadership wants to know whether rolling out Claude Code improved engineering productivity. Which metric is the best evidence?
options: The number of lines of code generated by Claude Code each week
The share of Claude Code suggestions that developers accepted
Cycle time and change failure rate, compared with a pre-rollout baseline
The number of Claude Code sessions each developer starts per day
correct_answer: Cycle time and change failure rate, compared with a pre-rollout baseline
explanation: Productivity claims need outcome metrics compared with a baseline, such as cycle time paired with a quality measure like change failure rate (C). Lines generated (A), suggestions accepted (B), and session counts (D) are vanity metrics: each can rise without any improvement in what ships.

text: Overnight, time to first token doubles and input token cost rises about 4x for an assistant. Traffic is steady. What should on-call check first?
options: Whether the retrieval index was refreshed overnight with new documents
The `cache_read_input_tokens` metric and recent commits to the system prompt
Whether the provider has lowered the rate limits on the organization's account overnight
Whether users started asking longer and more complex questions overnight
correct_answer: The `cache_read_input_tokens` metric and recent commits to the system prompt
explanation: A sudden jump in both latency and input cost with steady traffic is the signature of a broken prompt cache, often a dynamic value added to the static prefix. Check `cache_read_input_tokens` and diff recent prompt commits (B). An index refresh (A) shows up as wrong answers, not a 4x cost jump. Rate limits (C) produce 429 errors, not higher token cost. Question length (D) would not change overnight with steady traffic.
